note: Article and topic proposals. Every title here is a question, because that is the shape the brief asks for and the shape the site already does well. Each one rests on a fact that was read off an official page on 2026-11-17, and the source is printed next to it. What is NOT here, and will not be invented: no search volume, no trend ranking, no 'people also ask' count, no claim that one of these is more popular than another. The brief offers its four working titles as hypotheses and is explicit that they are not claims about popularity, and the site's own evidence rule for trending claims forbids the alternative. Until BQ2-10 closes there is no instrument that could rank these, so any ordering here would be decoration.
ranking_note: Deliberately unordered. Ordering these would imply a measurement that has not been taken.

rows.working_title: Basket or oven-style air fryer: what should you compare?
rows.why_this_shape: It is the first decision a buyer actually faces, and the product set answers it three different ways — so the page can compare instead of describe.
rows.rests_on: The three air-fryer destinations span both forms: a 6-quart twin-basket machine (BD-09), a 26-quart French-door oven (BD-10) and an 8-quart single basket (BD-11).
rows.status: proposed — the shape exists, the page that puts the two side by side does not

rows.working_title: A no-hype checklist for comparing air fryer capacity
rows.why_this_shape: Capacity is the number every listing leads with and the one buyers most often misread, because a 6-quart twin basket and a 6-quart single basket are not the same cooking space.
rows.rests_on: The published capacity figures, each read from the listing and the manufacturer page rather than from the marketing headline: 6 quarts across two independent 3-quart baskets (BD-09), 26 quarts (BD-10), 8 quarts (BD-11).
rows.status: proposed — a checklist page is a different page from the one that exists

rows.working_title: How to assess cleanup and counter-space trade-offs
rows.why_this_shape: The existing fit guide addresses counter space, while a cleanup guide would need to add verified care details rather than repeat the dimensions. The earlier copy asserted a buyer-regret popularity ranking that no source in this register supports; it was removed 2026-11-19 (T68).
rows.rests_on: The site's existing counter-space analysis and manufacturer care instructions, where available. Cleanup claims must be verified from the official product pages or manuals before publication.
rows.status: proposed — the counter-space half is published, the cleanup half is not

rows.working_title: Questions to ask before buying a multi-function kitchen appliance
rows.why_this_shape: The brief offers this title and it is the one that survives the category question — it is answerable whichever way BQ2-11 goes, because it is about the buyer's decision rather than about a product type.
rows.rests_on: The two new products name five cooking environments between them, and one of them names air frying in its own listing title (BD-04), which is the honest bridge between the two halves of the product set.

rows.working_title: Instant-read or wireless: what are you actually paying for?
rows.why_this_shape: It is the first decision a thermometer buyer faces, and the two products in this set sit on opposite sides of it — so the page can be a comparison rather than two reviews.
rows.rests_on: One destination is a one-second instant-read thermometer with an auto-rotate bright LED screen and no wireless function named in its title (BD-03); the other is a wireless thermometer with WiFi unlimited range and three ultra-thin probes (BD-04).
rows.existing_page: none — no page on the site mentions a thermometer

rows.working_title: How many probes does a meat thermometer need?
rows.why_this_shape: Probe count is the specification that most changes how a thermometer is used and the one a first-time buyer has no intuition for.
rows.rests_on: One product's listing names three ultra-thin probes (BD-04); the other is a single-probe instant read (BD-03).

rows.working_title: What does 'NIST certified' mean on a thermometer box?
rows.why_this_shape: Both listings put a certification mark in the title. Explaining a specification the buyer cannot evaluate is exactly the added value the anti-thin-affiliation guidance asks for.
rows.rests_on: Both destination listings state NIST or NSF certification in the product title as served (BD-03: 'NIST&NSF Certified'; BD-04: '1000°F Heat Safe | 5 Sensors').
rows.status: proposed — blocked by BS-03, and it needs an official definition of the certification to be read before it is written

rows.working_title: Do you need an app to cook a steak?
rows.why_this_shape: It is a real objection, not a feature list, and it is the question a buyer asks after they have already decided they want a thermometer.
rows.rests_on: One product's listing names WiFi unlimited range via an app and a 1000°F heat-safe probe (BD-04); the other names an auto-rotate LED screen and no app (BD-03).

rows.working_title: The two tools that decide whether dinner is cooked
rows.why_this_shape: It is the only title here that turns the site's awkward product set into an asset rather than a problem: an air fryer cooks it, a thermometer tells you when it is done, and a site that sells both can say something a single-category site cannot.
rows.rests_on: One of the two thermometers names 'Air Fryer' among the cooking environments in its own listing title (BD-04), alongside BBQ, grill, oven and smoker.
rows.status: proposed — the most interesting title here and the most dependent on BS-03

rows.working_title: What we could not verify, and why we left it blank
rows.why_this_shape: It is the page the site is already unusually good at, and it is the one no competitor has. It also directly serves the brief's own instinct to grow on the verification angle rather than on volume.
rows.rests_on: The five product-intent rows on board/products.html, ten of whose fields are empty on purpose.
